plate_findings.evidence: Caption identifies left-sided proptosis in a patient with CCF.
The clinical image visibly shows prominent abnormal conjunctival/episcleral vessels; the article describes corkscrew episcleral blood vessels associated with CCF.
Caption states that imaging showed enlargement of the superior ophthalmic vein.
The caption describes dilated serpiginous intraconally and cavernous-sinus signal-void structures in the MRI panels, including C.
Caption states that enlarged extraocular muscles were present on the left side, demonstrated by axial MRI in panels E and F.
The caption states that MRA and MRV confirmed the diagnosis of CCF.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: Clinical photograph of the affected left eye showing proptosis, conjunctival chemosis and abnormal episcleral vessels in a patient with confirmed CCF. B: Close clinical view of the left conjunctiva demonstrates chemosis and abnormal vascularity characteristic of the CCF described in the caption. C: Axial MRI demonstrates the left-sided superior ophthalmic vein enlargement and abnormal orbital/cavernous-sinus vascular channels attributed to CCF. D: MRI panel shows abnormal serpiginous flow-void vessels in the left orbit extending toward the cavernous sinus, a characteristic CCF finding. E: Axial MRI demonstrates left extraocular-muscle enlargement, a described manifestation of CCF in this patient. F: Coronal MRI shows left-sided extraocular-muscle enlargement as explicitly attributed to the patient's CCF. G: MRA/MRV image demonstrates marked left superior ophthalmic vein enlargement and confirms the CCF diagnosis in the same...

panels.figure_caption: This 17-year-old male presented with sudden development of decreased vision in the left eye, proptosis, conjunctival chemosis, ptosis and elevated intraocular pressure 1 year after having experienced head trauma (A, B). Imaging studies revealed classic features of CCF on the left side manifested as evidence of the enlargement of the superior ophthalmic vein (SPV)(C). Dilated signal-void serpiginous structures are seen intraconally and extending to the left cavernous sinus (C, D). In addition, there were enlarged extraocular muscles on the left side, as evidenced by axial and cornonal MRI (E, F). MRA and MRV confirmed the diagnosis of CCF with markedly enlarged left SOV (G)

One may expect restricted ocular motility and diplopia as a result of enlargement of extraocular muscles; and exposure keratopathy as a result of proptosis (Figures 3E and 3F). Direct and indirect CCFs most commonly cause the classic triad of proptosis, conjunctival chemosis and cranial bruit but can masquerade as chronic conjunctivitis (Figures 1–3). Unruptured aneurysms can compress the third cranial nerve and the anterior visual pathways. Ruptured aneurysms and subarachnoid hemorrhage can result in Terson syndrome and papilledema. Arteriovenous malformations, with or without hemorrhage, may compress portions of the retrochiasmal pathways, causing visual field loss.
